title: Sustainable Agriculture: Foundations
welcome_lead: Compare monoculture with crop rotation, organic farming and integrated pest management.
meta_desc: GCSE Environmental Science adventure on sustainable agriculture foundations: rotation, organic, IPM.

concepts.def: Growing single crop on large area each year.
Cycling crops by year to maintain soil and yields.
Integrated Pest Management using mixed methods.
Crop grown to protect and enrich soil between seasons.
Legumes adding nitrogen to soil with bacteria.

walkthroughs.body_html: Monoculture maximises short-term efficiency but depletes soil nutrients, encourages pests adapted to that crop, and increases need for fertilisers and pesticides. The Irish potato famine (1845) showed catastrophic risk of single-variety dependence. Modern monocultures of wheat, maize and soy dominate global cropland and contribute to biodiversity decline.

Crop rotation cycles different crops on the same land. Classic UK four-field rotation alternated wheat, turnips, barley and clover. Clover and other legumes fix nitrogen via Rhizobium bacteria, restoring fertility. Modern rotations include cover crops to protect soil, suppress weeds and trap nutrients. Rotation reduces pest cycles and fertiliser need.

IPM combines biological control (ladybirds for aphids), cultural methods (rotation, planting dates), physical barriers, and pesticides only as last resort. It cuts pesticide use, protects pollinators and beneficial predators, and slows resistance. Pheromone traps monitor pests, helping growers time interventions precisely.
